wǣron fullfręmede = were completed/finished; the coordinated subject is the heavens, the earth, and all their array. wǣron is a familiar form but this use with a participle remains supplied.
Eornostlice = accordingly/thus; ðā = then, an adverb rather than the identically spelled article. No article form is being parsed at those tokens.
eall hiera frætwung = all their array; eall modifies feminine singular frætwung. fram eallum ðǣm weorce = from all the work; eallum and ðǣm agree with neuter dative singular weorce.
ðone seofoðan dæg = the seventh day: masculine accusative singular with the actual weak ordinal form seofoðan. No other ordinal forms are required.

on ðone seofoðan dæg = on the seventh day; on ðone dæg = on that day/the day just named. These are temporal phrases with accusative. Do not replace dæg with dative dæge or infer motion. Unit 1 locative on + dative does not license this use.

ðe introduces which/that clauses referring to work: which he made; which he performed; which he created to make. The relative particle represents the direct object within each clause, although its antecedents weorc, weorce, weorces have different external cases. Supply clause boundaries and this relation; do not assign general relative syntax.

Here geręstan + reflexive pronoun + fram-phrase means rest from work. fram governs dative weorce. The form of fram and separation use were taught in Unit 1, but that contract confined independent use to a supplied separating frame.
for-ðon-ðe introduces the reason: because he ceased from his work on that day. The clause continues through the final supplied relative/infinitive phrase.

geswāc his weorces = ceased from his work. geswāc governs genitive weorces; his is its possessive genitive, not a second direct object. The known genitive form does not imply this new government was taught.

ðe hē gescēop tō wyrceanne = which he created to make. Cook gives Latin creavit ut faceret and the margin rendering created to make. tō wyrceanne is an inflected infinitive indicating the making for which he created the work. Preserve the actual source relation; do not silently substitute created and made or finished creating. This compact calque is supplied whole, with no independent infinitive target or unique idiomatic-translation demand.
Adjectives agree with their own noun/referent in case, number and gender; attributive and ordinary positive predicate uses are taught.
Complete selected strong N/G/D/A singular/plural in all genders; lexical alternations and distinct reference instrumentals are identified.
Complete selected weak N/G/D/A singular/plural; ordinary genitive plural -ra and explicitly audited comparative exceptions.
Long adjective stems: zero feminine nominative singular and neuter N/A plural in selected monosyllabic strong paradigms.
Short adjective stems: selected -u in feminine nominative singular and neuter N/A plural; complete lexical paradigms determine spelling.
glæd alternates æ/a in its checked cells; this is not an unrestricted substitution rule.
Selected disyllabic stems and vowel loss are taught together with exceptions; preserve the audited cell rather than delete every medial vowel.
Complete -e adjective pattern represented by æppelbǣre, distinguishing lexical -e from case endings.
Complete gearu pattern with checked u/w alternation.
Complete hēah pattern, including h loss and the selected contraction before endings.

Ordinary attributive adjectives are weak after article/demonstrative; bare ordinary adjectives are strong. After possessives Cook permits strong and sometimes weak; no universal possessive→weak rule and no new rule for adjectives after limiting genitives.
Ordinary positive predicative adjectives are strong and nominative, agreeing with the subject even when its noun phrase contains an article. Comparatives remain weak.
Recognize distinct masculine/neuter singular strong adjective and demonstrative instrumental citations; no instrumental construction is independently taught.
The six agreeing possessives have complete strong morphology. Their endings agree with the possessed noun, not the possessor; personal-genitive citations retain separate records.
Choose mīn/ðīn/uncer/incer/ūre/ēower for the possessor person/number, then inflect for the possessed head. Contrast prior invariant his/hiere/hiera. No self or sīn teaching.
Regular lēof/lēofra/lēofost series, with full assigned degree inflections.
eald/ieldra/ieldest is the assigned umlaut series; no universal umlaut instruction.
Complete selected gōd, yfel, micel and lȳtel comparison series; exact stems and superlative choices are lexical.
Comparatives are weak attributively and predicatively; full paradigms include transparently derived genitive plural contractions and licensed -ena selections.
Full strong/weak superlative morphology; ordinary attributive superlatives normally weak, taught predicate use strong. Partitive/substantival uses remain unassigned.
Bounded subject A + copula + comparative + ðonne + parallel subject B: B is nominative, with repeated copula understood. No generalized comparative-clause or genitive-standard syntax.
Selected supplied adjective citations wīd/swīð/sōð yield checked -e/-lice adverbs; no full adjective system implied by these citation bases.
Selected adverbs qualify actions or whole statements without case/number/gender agreement; sōðlice truly is distinct from the supplied source connective sense.
swīðe very qualifies an adjective; adverb has no adjective-agreement ending.
wīde/wīdor/wīdost and wel/bęt/bętst are invariant adverbial degrees; no new comparative-clause syntax.
Complete ān singular cardinal forms with singular count nouns; plural reference cells confer no productive plural-one sense.
Complete twēgen/ðrīe N/G/D/A plural across genders; no noun dual paradigm.
Checked cardinal 4–12 forms used invariantly before plural count nouns; no postposed/substantival inflection or higher-number partitive syntax.
Cardinal one with singular nouns, 2–12 with plural count nouns; numeral gender/case agrees where the selected system inflects.
Complete selected first, third–seventh weak paradigms express order. Ordinary noun case is supplied by already taught syntax; no temporal on+accusative production implied.
ōðer second remains strong even after the article; selected syncope and feminine ōðru with valid variants are explicit.
Complete ðes/ðēos/ðis system: this/these, agreeing with the noun in N/G/D/A; reference instrumentals do not create syntax milestones.
Existing se/sēo/ðæt morphology now also expresses pointing that/those; relative and general third-person pronoun uses remain unassigned.
Complete new ðing heavy-neuter paradigm in the sense thing/things; prior ordinary case constructions apply.
Counted lēoht luminary distinct from mass light; prior singular morphology retained and all four plural cases promoted to production.
Direct speech introduced by supplied cwæð, with then and connective sōðlice. Unit2 productive quotation was specifically with sęcgan.
Plural finite optatives express a wish/command. Bēon is not an infinitive; all coordinated verbs share the lights as subject.
on governs dative fæstnesse; ðǣre heofonan is embedded genitive feminine singular, from weak heofone.
tō + dative expresses assigned function/purpose. Noun cells are prior; this prepositional use is not taught by Unit2 tō wyrceanne.
Resultative fulfillment formula; prior wæs form does not establish independent perfect/resultative syntax.
gesętte has omitted God/he subject; hīe is accusative plural object. on ðǣre heofonan has dative feminine singular heofonan, not genitive.
ðæt introduces purpose; scinen, gīemden, tōdǣlden are past optatives. This is not the content-that sense.
ofer eorðan means over the earth. Source spelling eorðan is compatible with accusative or dative singular; do not require one uniquely.
gīeman governs genitive in this exact construction, explicitly documented by §156f. Genitive forms themselves are prior.
Supplied strong geseah plus content clause ðæt hit gōd wæs. New predicate-adjective morphology can be observed within supplied content-clause syntax.
Closing resultative formula and source word order supplied. The new ordinal fēorða agrees with dæg; męrgen is a source vowel variant of selected morgen.
Identify the four principal-part positions and distinguish finite preterite entries from supplied infinitive/participle citations.

Audited dental/sibilant contractions, ð-stem effects, geminate reduction and bounded g/h variants in selected present2/3sg.

Complete Class II tēon draw/pull indicative, with its selected contracted present and tēah/tuge/tugon past.
Select fand as past1sg, funde as past2sg and usual past3sg, fundon for all plural persons; admit first-person funde and third-person fand as documented alternatives.
Recognize complete bregdan and composite fēolan indicative references using displayed tables and their declared source/variant limits.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: Ordinary weorðan become takes a nominative predicate adjective agreeing with its subject.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: Prior preverbal ne extends explicitly to the selected noncontracting strong indicatives.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: Use the assigned strong preterites for successive past events in independent coordinated clauses, retaining prior subject agreement and direct quotation.
The ship breaks up with tōberstan and the companions perish with forweorðan; each is an intransitive subject–verb clause.
Ðǣr-tō-ēacan means in addition to that/besides: further winds join the already described storm. The preceding storm is summarized in separate English editorial context.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Fixed connective supplied; no productive compound-adverb rule.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: him ongēan stōd = stood against/opposed them. ongēan follows its dative pronoun. The natural local reading takes him as the preceding northeast winds, but its spelling also permits masculine/neuter singular and the antecedent is an editorial inference, not morphologically unique.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Do not demand unique number/antecedent identification from him alone; do not teach general postposition syntax. A justified alternative antecedent is not rejected solely for differing from the guiding inference.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: ðæt scip eall = the whole ship/all the ship. eall is strong neuter nominative singular, postposed to the subject noun phrase; its morphology/sense were recognition-only in Unit3.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Keep eall morphology and sense at their prior recognition milestone; the postposed whole/all construction is supplied, not independent production.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Prior spatial on+dative does not automatically establish every figurative/circumstantial sense.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: Apollonius gefēran = Apollonius’s companions. Cook note1 explicitly identifies the foreign proper name here as genitive despite its -us appearance. gefēran is nominative plural, not a subject named Apollonius.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: The relation and before-head placement are prior; the actual foreign-name case form is supplied. No complete Latin-name declension is introduced.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Prior recognition of ealle is not new productive quantifier mastery.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: forwurdon tō dēaðe = perished to death, naturally all died/perished. dēaðe is masculine dative singular; tō states the endpoint/result, not an infinitive marker or the previously supplied function-for sense.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Supply this tō phrase whole; no general goal/result construction is assumed.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: Apollonius āna = Apollonius alone. āna is weak masculine nominative singular of ān in its alone sense, agreeing with the sole survivor; it is not cardinal one or the homographic feminine plural reference form.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: New sense and weak form are supplied only; Unit3 productive cardinal ān does not cover them.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: becōm mid sunde = came/arrived by swimming. sund is a neuter noun; sunde is dative singular after mid. This means phrase is not an infinitive or newly productive instrumental construction.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Supply actual mid sunde; do not infer a productive swimming verb or general mid syntax.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: tō Pentapolim ðǣm Cyreniscan lande = to Pentapolis, the Cyrenian land. The foreign place name occupies the destination position; the native appositional phrase is neuter dative singular, with weak Cyreniscan. Preserve the foreign -im spelling rather than treating it as a native OE accusative-governance rule.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Exact destination/apposition is supplied. No general foreign-name declension or productive tō-goal syntax.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: and ðǣr ūpēode on ðǣm strande = and there he came/went up onto the shore. Apollonius remains the understood subject. ūpēode is the actual anomalous preterite of ūpgān; strande is masculine dative singular in the printed local on phrase.
all_actual_feature_boundaries.scope_note: Supply ūpēode and ðǣr; preserve dative strande and do not replace it with accusative from a modern English motion gloss.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: Present and preterite subjunctive each have one singular form for all3persons and one plural form for all3persons. Selected normal endings -e/-en; contracted/anomalous rows explicit. Full672cells+6bēo alternatives.

Use present stem without indicative2/3sg umlaut; use strong preterite plural stem in both subjunctive numbers. Weak past retains its dental stem. Present subjunctive preterite-presents use lexical plural-type/umlauted forms, not strong indicative singular.

Independent present subjunctive expresses wishes/exhortations, including thirdperson Let... and firstplural Letus.... Secondperson imperative and subjunctive are formally/syntactically distinct even where spellings coincide. English let here is not a new lǣtan causative construction.

Open gif clauses can use indicative. A contextually tentative/hypothetical request can use present subjunctive, followed by an imperative or ordinary indicative main clause. Gif itself never licenses an automatic conversion rule.
With explicit unreal/nonpast context and supplied interpretation, preterite subjunctive can refer to nonpast events. No rigid unscaffolded English would template or all counterfactual types assigned.

Keep learned mæg capability, mōt permission, wille/wolde volition distinct from inflectional subjunctive wishes. A past spelling does not mechanically mean English would/might; willan is not automatically future. Preserve bounded earlier cunnan/ðurfan/durran/sculan senses.

Complete present/past formation pairs for12selected lemmas; other roster citations remain audit-only. Source libbendu/flēogendu/swimmendu receive recognition with full mapped -ende pattern; participial accompaniment cweðende remains locally supplied syntax.
Full48NGDA strong/weak cells per selected model; attributive participles follow adjective choice and agreement. Distinguish predicate participles, which may be uninflected or strong-masculine-like.

For assigned accusative-object verbs, present or preterite wesan/bēon or weorðan + past participle expresses passive. Finite auxiliary agrees with the nominative subject. Agent omitted in productive tasks; no new fram-agent rule needed. Wesan often presents state/result and weorðan event, but not an absolute contrast or one-to-one English tense mapping.
Wæs geworden in Creation is become/come-to-pass resultative close, not a transitive passive. Perfects/progressives/absolutes remain outside independent production.

Active hātan naming can take object accusative + name/predicate accusative. Ordinary periphrastic passive (ge)hāten derives from the checked participle+auxiliary rule; inherited hātte remains audit-only.
Promote eall strong NGDA and introduce image-checked longǣlc strong NGDA. Complete models do not teach unrelated indefinite pronouns, partitives, adverbial quantifier idioms or weak paradigms.
Rule over the genitive object.

all_actual_feature_boundaries.description: Complete twelve-cell indicative systems of wyrcean, gīeman, rīcsian, gemanigfieldan and tōtwǣman, preserving their individually taught lexical scope.
Complete second-singular and second-plural imperative of tōtwǣman; accusative separated thing and fram+dative landmark.

Spatial ofer permits the source-attested accusative/dative constructions. Fulk§36 explicitly verifies both governments; exact eorðan is syncretic, so its surface alone cannot prove either case. Authority ofer+accusative is separately taught. No unrestricted case interchange or exceptionless motion/rest rule is assigned.
A separate dative beneficiary can accompany a copular clause with tō+dative assigned function, as ēow tō męte; the beneficiary is not a possessive adjective.

Nū now, swā so, ðus thus, ēac also and swilce likewise are invariant adverbs; efne behold introduces a statement as an interjection. Nū is may precede its nominal subject in the given presentational frame. The conjunction swilce as if is unassigned.
The learned second-person imperative or new present subjunctive of the auxiliary combines with the selected past participle to command or wish a passive situation. The participle is nonfinite.
Previously taught direct quotation now includes the independently taught subjunctive wish/exhortation and basic conditional. Quoted pronouns belong to the quoted speaker’s setting.
In verbal predicates a past participle may be uninflected or take strong-masculine-like endings: neuter plural dēor bunden/bundene are both licensed. Attributive agreement remains a different target.
Selected full-vowel participial agreement models coexist with listed syncope variants; weak dental principal parts are lexical and cannot uniformly be recovered as past-minus-e.
Supply tēon ... forð / tugon forð as bring forth. The finite morphology may be taught, but draw/pull does not automatically supply this lexical sense.
Supply cucu on līfe as alive, with exact irregular cucu. It is not the ordinary locative on frame alone.
Supply ðe ðā wæteru tugon forð on hiera hīwum, which the waters brought forth in their forms/kinds. ðe is accusative object and waters nominative subject.
Supply on hiera hīwum and æfter hiera cynne as in their forms/kinds and according to their kind; no general new prepositional production.
Supply God geseah ðā ðæt hit gōd wæs as God then saw that it was good. Content conjunction, clause boundary and source verb-final order remain supplied.
Supply ðus cweðende as saying thus, accompanying God’s blessing. The participial form is productive, but this accompanying-action construction is not independently assigned.
Supply the continuation And blētsode hīe: God remains the subject and hīe is the accusative plural object; the exact plain blētsian is distinct from productive geblētsian.
Singular-only common masculine/feminine and neuter hwā/hwæt NGDA; hwǣm primary, hwām valid variant. Distinct instrumental forms are reference only.
Question pronouns take the case their own function requires: subject nominative, possessor genitive, object accusative, recipient or governed dative.
Full strong hwilc/hwæðer/hūlic agreement in ordinary direct questions; hwæðer specifies two alternatives. No weak interrogative-adjective system assigned.

Direct yes/no questions commonly begin with the finite verb; wh-words or phrases commonly precede the finite verb, and a wh-subject is itself the subject. No English dummy do is added. These are tendencies, not an exceptionless V2 transformation.
Lexical hū how and hwȳ why in direct questions; hwȳ does not establish general instrumental syntax.
A finite verb commonly occurs early in an independent clause and later, often final, in a dependent/relative clause. Count constituents rather than words; avoid an obligatory order formula.
Ilca same is weak only; ordinarily article + ilca and weak agreement of any following adjective.

Self agrees with its referent; use strong/weak forms in ordinary emphasis, or add agreeing self to a personal reflexive accusative/dative. In Ic nęrie mē selfne the male speaker is both agent and object; selfne agrees with mē.

Ordinary attributive sum some/a certain, ǣnig any in questions, gehwilc each with singular noun, and swilc such; complete strong morphology. Following ordinary descriptive adjective in swilc phrases is strong. Extended negative/distributive/partitive/correlative constructions deferred.
Apply prior strong ōðer morphology to ordinary other/another, including after article; distinguish prior second sense.
Invariant ðe introduces an ordinary relative clause and can represent different internal case functions; it is not an English personal interrogative pronoun.
The inflected se/sēo/ðæt series can introduce relative clauses alone or followed by ðe; reuse its full NGDA morphology with newly taught relative function.

In selected productive relative clauses, gender and number track the antecedent while relative case is governed by its function within its own clause. An antecedent in dative can have a nominative relative, and vice versa; this is the selected ordinary construction, not a universal ban on attraction.

A relative subject with a personal-pronoun antecedent can carry that antecedent's person: ðū + ðe ... hulpe/gescēope takes second singular. Number/person must follow the intended antecedent, not the English word who.
Recognize that an inflected relative sometimes takes its antecedent's case rather than the case expected from its own internal function. No independent production of case attraction is assigned.
Recognize ðe plus a personal pronoun as an attested less common relative strategy; its inflected personal member marks the internal function. Full independent use deferred.
Recognize singular-only gehwā/gehwæt and its NGDA forms as an indefinite ge- compound. Independent indefinite/distributive syntax remains Unit15.
Productive ordinary countable lives with all plural līf/līfa/līfum/līf cells; retain prior formal-recognition history.

Libban may have the cognate accusative līf life, as in live our lives; the agreeing possessive is plural accusative. This is a bounded lexical construction, not permission to add objects to all intransitives.

Habban + accusative controlled entity + on + dative possessive/gewealde means have under one's control. On takes dative in this established control frame; spatial under is not mechanically substituted.
Promote gefyllan fill with an accusative thing/place filled. Earlier finish sense and source-only fill exposure do not establish independent fill production until this unit.
Complete present/preterite indicative and subjunctive of weakII ætēowian; selected i spellings retained.
Ætēowian is intransitive appear; the thing becoming visible is the nominative subject. Do not substitute transitive ætīewan display.
Complete scīnan present scīne/scīnen and preterite scine/scinen subjunctive systems, all persons; preserve two earlier supplied histories.
Both geblētsian commands: singular geblētsa, plural geblētsiað; direct-address target according to the prompt.
Cook I.8.13 supplies gesęte as a singular command; assign that exact support plus the local in-sea phrase. No full gesettan command or placement-government system follows from a parenthetic hint.

productive_outcomes: Use the assigned lexical gender; do not infer it from English or from a bare nominative ending alone.
Coordinate nominal phrases with and; each article agrees with its own head.
Strong masculine consonant stems: complete N/G/D/A singular and plural; assign only the listed lexical senses.
Strong masculine -e: replace the nominative -e appropriately; no invented mętees.
Complete dæg and hwæl patterns, with æ in singular and a in plural; do not extend to clusters such as wæstm.
Complete selected fugol and morgen patterns; loss of medial vowel with endings and lexical diagnostic forms. Source variants remain valid.
Complete hof and sǣd patterns; short-stem monosyllabic neuter N/A plural -u versus heavy-stem zero; explain geminates and clusters.
Complete trēo paradigm with w before endings and selected exceptional N/A plural trēowu.
Complete selected ǣfen, tācen, wæter, nīeten patterns; retain or syncopate medial vowel as documented, not by an unrestricted weight rule.
Complete long-stem strong feminine pattern; selected N/A plural -a, with source -e variants noted separately.
Complete selected tīd and wyrt patterns; endingless accusative singular despite ordinary -e feminine obliques.
Complete -nes pattern; -ness- in obliques/plural, retaining e; apply to each listed diagnostic stem.
Complete selected -ung/-ing feminine pattern, productive -e singular obliques; source -a variants separately noted.
Complete weak masculine steorra and weak feminine eorðe patterns; contrast all singular/plural cases.
Complete mann: męnn dative singular and nominative/accusative plural; other selected cases as listed.
Complete selected niht paradigm, including genitive singular niht and endingless nominative/accusative plural.
Complete selected sea table, with productive attested cells and explicitly supplied reconstructed genitive plural *sǣwa.
Complete selected plural-only darkness paradigm; no singular invented.
Produce the selected article forms agreeing with their own noun in gender, number and nominative/genitive/dative/accusative case.
Produce every person/number cell of the present eom/eart/is/sindon and preterite wæs/wǣre/wæs/wǣron indicative series.
Finite subjects and noun predicates identifying the subject are nominative; ordinary bare noun predicates need no translated indefinite article.
Use the copula's appropriate number/person in the taught ordinary clauses.
Produce limiting relational genitives. Follow Cook's exercise target: dependent first, head noun without its own article; retain the dependent's required article.
Select accusative direct-object noun/article forms in explicitly supplied transitive finite-verb frames.
Use taught locative on with dative ('in/on'); this is a selected construction, not a universal spatial rule.
Use fram plus dative for the entity from which something is separated, in an explicitly supplied separating frame.
Preserve the head's externally governed case while its own limiting dependent remains genitive; the genitive article belongs to that dependent.
Use a dative recipient and accusative thing given in the explicitly supplied sealde frame; distinguish to/for-recipient from the direct object.
recognition_outcomes: Recognize æ, interchangeable manuscript þ/ð, Cook's preference for ð, his hooked ę, and quantity marks; preserve exact printed quantities.
Distinguish long vowels/diphthongs from syllable weight due to two consonants or a geminate; apply only the stated noun-pattern domains.
Identical spellings may occupy different case/number cells; determine syntactic role from construction and agreement.
Recognize distinct instrumental masculine/neuter singular ðȳ and ðon as reference cells; no productive instrumental syntax.
Recognize that the opening On anginne gescēop God places the subject after the verb; parse by construction and forms, not English order alone.

clause_support.source_text: On anginne gescēop God heofonan and eorðan.

clause_support.source_text: and ðīestru wǣron ofer ðǣre nēowolnesse brādnesse;
support_notes: English darkness is normally singular; Old English ðīestru is plural and takes wǣron.

clause_support.source_text: and Godes gāst wæs gefęred ofer wæteru.

clause_support.source_text: God geseah ðā ðæt hit gōd wæs;
support_notes: geseah is unlengthened in this edition; hit refers to light.

clause_support.source_text: and hē gedǣlde ðæt lēoht fram ðǣm ðīestrum.

clause_support.source_text: And hēt ðæt lēoht Dæg, and ðā ðīestru Niht.
support_notes: Supply the understood subject he/God and the object/naming accusatives; the repeated verb is understood in the second half.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Present indicative has person-distinct singular and one form for allplural persons; weak preterite1/3sg coincide, 2sg adds -st to the selected1/3sg form, plural replaces its final e with on. No independent dual verb ending.

Selected present endings -e, -(e)st, -(e)ð, -að attach to the listed lexical stem. Gemination and i are retained in the 1sg/plural of short fręmman/nęrian types but absent in their 2/3sg. Longer diagnostic forms show the listed contraction and dental changes; do not infer each surface by merely appending the suffix to the infinitive.

audited_inflection_rules.domain: hīeran, gefyllan and comparable lexical assignments
audited_inflection_rules.rule: Class I -de with retained stem vowel; doubled consonant simplifies before the dental: fyllan→fylde, not fyllde. Short fręmman instead takes -ede and is a distinct lexical family.
ff/pp/ss dental preterites take -te and simplify gemination; tt type sęttan has sętte. Present2/3sg and past can coincide, but their analysis differs.

audited_inflection_rules.domain: sęndan versus lǣdan; geręstan versus mētan
audited_inflection_rules.rule: Consonant+d has sęnde versus vowel+d lǣdde; consonant+t has geręste versus vowel+t mētte. Preserve the lexical quantity; vowel length does not itself license deleting a dental.
Dental d becomes t after the relevant voiceless final: īecte. This differs from lexical irregular wyrc(e)an→worhte, which changes the stem and c to h.

The past is gierede. Cook allows present w retained or lost; the selected complete table retains w in1sg/plural and uses w-less full endings in2/3sg. This is disclosed selection, not allpresent w deletion.
Learn the diagnostic past stem with the lexeme: sęllan→sealde; gewyrcean→geworhte. Other §114 verbs are not silently assigned; the rule is not a free prediction from modern English.

gefręmman→gefręmede, ęfnan→ęfnede (source alternative ęfnde), nęrian→nęrede. lęcgan is an explicitly recorded exception (lęgde/lēde); no recall target. hyngran is impersonal and not substituted into personal sentences.
Use -ie,-ast,-að,-iað present; -ode,-odest,-odon selected past. Cook also prints -edon plural and other past-ending variants. -ian alone cannot distinguish II from short I; class is lexical.
Allfour survivors are separate complete systems: habban, libban, sęcgan, hycgan. Their present stem changes and selected past stems are not generated by the single lufian template.

Personal pronouns provide reflexive case forms. Selected productive frame geręstan + accusative self-coreferential pronoun; the same personal case form can otherwise refer to another entity. Form alone does not establish coreference.
Third-person genitives his/hiere/hiera are invariant. First/second genitive cells are not permission to use the corresponding inflecting possessive adjective without its later adjective paradigm.

Place ne immediately before the finite verb in the selected ordinary weak clauses. Complete nabban forms are recognition-only; ne+habban contraction is frequent, not compulsory. Negative copula and concord are not assigned.

constructions.support: wǣron fullfręmede = were completed/finished; the coordinated subject is the heavens, the earth, and all their array. wǣron is a familiar form but this use with a participle remains supplied.
Eornostlice = accordingly/thus; ðā = then, an adverb rather than the identically spelled article. No article form is being parsed at those tokens.
eall hiera frætwung = all their array; eall modifies feminine singular frætwung. fram eallum ðǣm weorce = from all the work; eallum and ðǣm agree with neuter dative singular weorce.
ðone seofoðan dæg = the seventh day: masculine accusative singular with the actual weak ordinal form seofoðan. No other ordinal forms are required.

on ðone seofoðan dæg = on the seventh day; on ðone dæg = on that day/the day just named. These are temporal phrases with accusative. Do not replace dæg with dative dæge or infer motion. Unit 1 locative on + dative does not license this use.

ðe introduces which/that clauses referring to work: which he made; which he performed; which he created to make. The relative particle represents the direct object within each clause, although its antecedents weorc, weorce, weorces have different external cases. Supply clause boundaries and this relation; do not assign general relative syntax.

Each of the six verbs is third-person singular preterite indicative. Their finite paradigms/senses must be taught before the reading; local support must not substitute for those missing prerequisites.
hiera is a plural possessor of array; his is masculine singular possessor of work. These genitive pronouns are indeclinable possessors and do not agree with the possessed noun's case.
hē geręste hine uses ordinary accusative hine reflexively. The later hine is an ordinary object whose masculine antecedent is dæg. Pronoun reference depends on the sentence, not the spelling alone.

Here geręstan + reflexive pronoun + fram-phrase means rest from work. fram governs dative weorce. The form of fram and separation use were taught in Unit 1, but that contract confined independent use to a supplied separating frame.
for-ðon-ðe introduces the reason: because he ceased from his work on that day. The clause continues through the final supplied relative/infinitive phrase.

geswāc his weorces = ceased from his work. geswāc governs genitive weorces; his is its possessive genitive, not a second direct object. The known genitive form does not imply this new government was taught.

ðe hē gescēop tō wyrceanne = which he created to make. Cook gives Latin creavit ut faceret and the margin rendering created to make. tō wyrceanne is an inflected infinitive indicating the making for which he created the work. Preserve the actual source relation; do not silently substitute created and made or finished creating. This compact calque is supplied whole, with no independent infinitive target or unique idiomatic-translation demand.

audited_inflection_rules.statement: Attributive and ordinary predicative adjectives agree in gender, number and case with their noun/referent; predicate positive adjectives are strong.
Ordinary adjective after demonstrative/article is weak; comparative always weak; ordinal weak except ōðer; superlative normally weak attributively and strong in the taught predicate use.

The six selected possessives decline strongly and agree with the possessed noun, not the owner. A following ordinary adjective may be strong or weak: Cook says sometimes weak; avoid imposing one universal choice.
Bounded A + copula + comparative + ðonne + B: when A and B are the contrasted subjects, B is nominative and the repeated copula may remain unexpressed. This does not cover every comparative clause.

Distinct strong adjective/demonstrative M/N singular instrumental forms are reference recognition only; agreement, manner, means, comparison-measure and prepositional instrumental syntax are not assigned. Weak instrumental shares dative forms, not an additional taught construction.

One modifies singular count nouns; two/three inflect for plural noun gender/case. Four through twelve are taught in ordinary uninflected pre-nominal use with plural count nouns and plural verb agreement. Plural ān is reference-only, weak āna alone unassigned.
Selected adjective bases yield -e or -lice adverbs; regular degree -or/-ost, with wel/bęt/bętst memorized separately. Adverbs are indeclinable and can qualify verbs/adjectives/other adverbs.

Use the selected lemma rows, not a universal instruction to delete medial vowels. Long disyllables often shorten before vowel endings but retain the medial vowel before consonantal -ne/-re/-ra; analogical and endingless-u alternatives are lexical/pattern choices.

independent_source_translation.text: God then said, “Let there now be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them separate day and night, and let them be for signs, for seasons, for days, and for years. And let them shine in the firmament of heaven and illuminate the earth”; it then came to pass thus. And God made two great lights: the greater light for the illumination of the day, and the lesser light for the illumination of the night; and he made stars. And he set them in heaven, so that they might shine over the earth, rule over the day and the night, and separate light and darkness; God then saw that it was good. And evening and morning came to pass, the fourth day.

recognition_outcomes: Recognize complete bregdan and feolan reference systems with their explicit evidence/derivation limits and no independent production requirement.
Distinguish selected forms from documented unselected alternatives, including first-person funde and third-person fand.
bounded_scope: No numbered Cook set is assigned in Unit4.
Only reviewed Unit1–3 milestones count as prior teaching.
All nonfinite principal parts are supplied citations; no infinitive, participial, perfect/passive or new mood construction follows.
Eall keeps its prior recognition status; its source quantifier uses are supplied. Āna alone is a separate supplied sense and weak form.
Ordinary weorðan become is separate from prior supplied passive weorthan-1. The existing wearð form is explicitly promoted with its supplied history retained.
No directional on rule, instrumental transport, productive prefix semantics or unbounded lexical government. No change to reference-only *sǣwa.
The source him antecedent is a contextual guiding inference, not a morphologically unique graded fact.

audited_inflection_rules.text: Use four principal parts. Present 1sg/pl use the present stem; present 2/3sg have the audited mutation/consonant changes. Past1/3sg normally share the singular stem; past2sg uses the plural stem plus -e, and all plural persons use -on. findan requires the separately printed exception.
Infinitive and past participle are citation/reference support only. No new perfect, passive, infinitive clause, participial agreement or prefix rule follows from a principal-parts table.
Class I normally ī : ā : i : i. Snīðan changes ð to d in plural-based past forms and participle. Contracted wrēon has a special present and h/g stems.
Class II normally ēo or ū : ēa : u : o. Present2/3sg ēo→īe and ū→ȳ; Cook also allows ī for īe. cēosan s/r, sēoðan ð/d, and tēon h/g are lexical changes.

III has several present/past-singular families, not one interchangeable vowel formula: bindan i/a/u/u, helpan e/ea/u/o, gieldan ie/ea/u/o, weorpan eo/ea/u/o, berstan e/æ/u/o. All those selected vowels are short. weorðan adds ð/d; winnan reduces nn; findan, bregdan and fēolan need explicit exception notes.

Dental d/t+ð gives tt (or t); d+st gives tst. s+st/ð gives st; ð before st may disappear and ð+ð may reduce. Geminates reduce before consonantal endings. g/h alternatives require the stated long-vowel/liquid environment; do not substitute h indiscriminately.

Cook permits full -est/-eð forms as well as syncopated cells. Their vowel can preserve an older mutated stem or be restored analogically; the audit selects complete contracted rows and records specifically checked variants rather than generating every possible full-ending spelling. A correct documented variant is not wrong merely for differing from the recall target.

Recognize present plural -e before an immediately following subject pronoun (Cook binde wē). This is conditioned by word order and is not a global alternative to -að after a preceding subject; production tasks may retain subject-before-verb.

Tōberstan and forweorðan are independently sourced lexemes, then expanded by identified base morphology. Their meanings and intransitive source frames are separate. No arbitrary prefix attachment or sense composition is licensed.
Extend prior preverbal ne to the introduced noncontracting strong indicatives. Keep negative copula, nillan and other contracted systems outside this extension.
Ordinary weorðan become can take a nominative predicate adjective agreeing with the subject. The finite indicative system does not promote old supplied passive constructions.

The finite paradigm does not establish object case. In particular helpan permits genitive or dative (selected dative here); bēodan command, gieldan repayment, bregdan instrumental use and other complements require separate teaching. Morphology-only verbs may be practised with person/tense labels without composing an unsupported clause.

local_support.text: Ðǣr-tō-ēacan = in addition to that/besides; the storm has already begun.
cōmon = came, third-person plural past of cuman (ClassIV); ēastnorðerne = northeasterly, masculine nominative plural.

angrīslica = fierce/raging; sūðwesterna = southwestern, both weak masculine nominative singular with wind. him ongēan stōd = stood against/opposed them: guiding reference, the northeast winds. eall = whole/all, neuter nominative singular agreeing with scip. This local quantifier use is supplied; its earlier morphology was recognition only.
on ðisse ęgeslican hrēohnesse = in this terrible storm: feminine dative singular; ęgeslican is weak after ðisse.
Apollonius before gefēran is genitive, Apollonius’s, as Cook note1 specifies. ealle = all, masculine nominative plural agreeing with the companions; quantifier use remains supplied.
tō dēaðe = to death, with dative singular dēaðe; the whole expression means that the companions died/perished.

The next Apollonius is nominative. āna = alone, weak masculine nominative singular, a distinct sense/form from cardinal one. becōm = came/arrived (third-person singular past, ClassIV). mid sunde = by swimming: dative noun sunde, not an infinitive.
tō Pentapolim ðǣm Cyreniscan lande = to Pentapolis, the Cyrenian land. Preserve the foreign name; the native apposition is neuter dative singular, with weak Cyreniscan.

ðǣr = there; ūpēode = he came/went up (anomalous past of ūpgān), with Apollonius understood. on ðǣm strande = on the shore, masculine dative singular as printed; do not replace the ending from the English gloss came ashore.

audited_inflection_rules.text: Present1sg -e and plural -að use the present stem; present2/3 require the selected mutation/consonant rules. Preterite1/3sg share the singular stem; preterite2sg uses the plural stem plus -e; all plural persons use -on. Contracted and j-present rows are explicit.
IV normally e/æ/ǣ/o. Learn niman nōm/nōmon and cuman cōm/cōmon separately; cuman present cymst/cymð.
V normally e/æ/ǣ/e. Separate palatal giefan, j-present biddan/licgan/sittan, etan longǣt, and contracted sēon/gesēon. cweðan changes ð to d in plural-based preterite and participle.

VI normally a/ō/ō/a, but j-present and palatal systems require the actual lexical rows. standan loses n in the past; slēan has short ie in present2/3 and g in past; scēop is a checked alternative to scōp.

Cook reduplicating verbs are course classVII: longēo or ē in the preterite, normally same present/participle vowel. wēpan/wōpen and fōn/fangen require explicit rows; hātan active is separate from hātte.
Preserve vowel quantity in umlaut: short ea→ie; longēa→īe; ā→ǣ;ō→ē. Dental combinations and geminate reduction are inherited rules. x plus either -st or -ð gives -xt: weaxan2/3sg both wiext.
biddan/licgan/sittan/hębban/scieppan have explicit consonant patterns; swęrian uses -ie/-est/-eð/-iað present endings like nęrian, but a strong swōr/swōron preterite.
geswīcan/scīnan/flēogan/swimman are new productive lexical systems applying already taught classesI–III. Prior supplied tokens are not prior mastery.
Four principal parts identify stems. Infinitives and participles remain supplied citations with no independent nonfinite recall or syntax; neither passive nor perfect follows from a table.
gesēon and gescieppan are independently evidenced lexemes. Prefix-preserving finite expansion is declared; arbitrary prefix attachment or semantic inference is not taught.

Finite morphology does not determine government. New composed clauses use only the bounded frames in lexical-frames.json and prior taught adjuncts; other selected verbs may be assessed by labelled morphology.

productive_outcomes: Use the complete present/preterite indicative systems of seven selected preterite-present and three anomalous verbs, with their exact changes and bounded elementary uses.

Use complete singular/plural imperative pairs for selected lexical models covering weak I–III, strong I–VII and needed anomalous patterns, including important exceptions and simple negative commands.
Use the selected plain/inflected infinitive pairs in elementary modal/volitional complements and bounded purposive cuman+tō constructions, retaining each lexical government.
Distinguish knowledge of a matter from learned ability, modal sense from morphological tense, and volition from completed action; use new and prior material in meaningful connected practice.
Complete all72 original graded tasks, read the checked controlled dialogue independently, and interpret the exact fisherman excerpt with its explicitly bounded support.
recognition_outcomes: Distinguish actual usable forms from uncertain or unattested modal citation labels; no regular modal imperative or inflected infinitive is invented.

Instrumental forms, plural ān and eall remain recognition/reference; *sǣwa remains a supplied starred reconstruction without milestones.

Diagnostic īecan, gierwan, ęfnan and hycgan lack arbitrary productive argument frames; use isolated form exercises unless a frame is expressly audited.
Hātan active indicative morphology does not teach hātte, infinitival causatives or double-accusative naming.

Prior source-only temporal/connective ðā, nū, ęft, swā, sōðlice, destination tō, motion on, mid and relative/content/purpose clauses remain supplied unless explicitly newly taught.
Simple ne negation extends only to newly audited systems; no negative copula, negative concord or every contracted negative form follows.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Selected preterite-presents have present 1sg=3sg, a special 2sg, and one plural stem/form for all persons; their past is weak. Learn each selected present/past pair as a complete indicative system.
Where Cook prints the past in -e followed by etc., the 2sg adds -st and the plural changes -e to -on. These are declared model-derived cells, not separately quoted textual tokens.
Don, gan, and willan have complete selected present/preterite indicative systems. Gan uses eode for the past; willan has wille in both present 1sg and 3sg, not an automatically added ordinary -ð.
The six beo/bist/bið/beoð indicative person cells supplement the prior wesan system and share its prior past; future or habitual/gnomic state depends on context.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Productive use is explicitly contextualized expected-later state; no new tense of every verb or future auxiliary willan is inferred.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Second singular commands address one person; second plural commands address more than one. The subject may be omitted or stated.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Only selected second-person systems are assigned. First/third-person optative commands remain later scope.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Ordinary strong singular imperative is the present stem without the infinitive ending; the second plural normally matches the present indicative plural. Present 2sg/3sg mutation is not mechanically imported into the command stem.

Contracted strong verbs restore final h in the singular command: wrīh, tēoh, seoh, sleah, fōh. The vowel qualities/quantities are lexical class patterns; seoh/sleah are short, wrīh/tēoh/fōh retain the selected long vowel. Their plurals remain contracted.

Heavy weak-I singular commands lack final -e; short/geminate-j patterns retain -e and lose the j-induced gemination in the singular: nęre/nęriað, fręme/fręmmað, sęle/sęllað, sęte/sęttað. Gierwan has giere/gierwað.
Selected heavy weak-I cys and gefyl simplify the final double consonant; plurals cyssað and gefyllað retain it. This is distinct from the short-stem -e model and from settan, whose singular is sete.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Final simplification is frequent and the selected normalized model; do not assert that all unsimplified final spellings are impossible.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Strong j-presents use weak-I-like -e singular commands: bide, site, lige, hęfe, sciepe, swęre; plurals retain their selected present stems. Hebban/hęfe and licgan/lige require their own consonant alternations.
Weak-II singular command changes -ian to -a; plural retains -iað: lufa/lufiað.
The selected complete weak-III pairs are hafa/habbað, leofa/libbað, saga/sęcgað, hoga/hycgað. Cook also gives sęge for saga and lifiað beside libbað, with optional e in sęcg(e)að/hycg(e)að.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Variants are documented reference alternatives, not automatic extra recall targets; nabban remains unassigned here.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Don has dō/dōð, gan gā/gāð; wesan/bēon gives wes/wesað and bēo/bēoð. No positive willan command pair or modal command pair is invented.
Cook notes shortened plural -e before an immediately following subject pronoun: binde gē, not bindað gē. This positional command variant is distinguished from indicative inversion.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Assigned commands omit the subject or use a preposed subject. No unrestricted plural -e production target, and no first/third-person command system.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: An earlier supplied dictionary citation does not constitute learned infinitive syntax. Only explicitly selected plain-infinitive cells are promoted; exact prior IDs may be retained with old analysis and history preserved.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Four defective modal headwords remain citation labels, with no infinitive/inflected target. Unselected earlier lexical rows get no milestone.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: For selected -an infinitives the course chooses -anne after tō; -ian therefore gives -ianne and geminated stems remain geminated. Contracted final -n gives -nne: fōnne, sēonne, dōnne, gānne, bēonne. The preposition tō is a separate token.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: -enne is a documented valid variant; selected -anne is not a universal grammatical requirement or a license to derive unattested modal cells.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: A finite selected modal/volitional verb takes a plain infinitive in the bounded same-subject construction; the finite verb marks person/number and present/past, while the infinitive does not agree.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: These lexical senses differ. Do not treat every modal as English must, or replace actual indicative past by an automatically hypothetical would/could reading.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Selected cuman + tō + inflected infinitive expresses the purpose of the same subject’s coming. Cook also documents bare infinitives with motion/specification/purpose.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: No claim that all purposes require tō; a valid bare-purpose alternative can miss the stated target without being ungrammatical. General accusative-and-infinitive and dependent-subject syntax remain outside scope.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Ordinary ne before a second-person imperative gives a negative command.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Construction only; the evidence does not teach ondrǣdan, its reflexive/genitive frame, or a nyllan imperative system.

audited_inflection_rules.claim: Source-local habban + tō-inflected infinitive describes something held/available for the named action.
audited_inflection_rules.boundary: Not a general rule translating all habban+tō as modern have to obligation, nor an assigned passive-infinitive system.

support_groups.local_meaning: Then, as soon as the fisherman saw that the young man was lying at his feet.
support_groups.scope_note: Supply the whole temporal frame and embedded content clause, with geonga/fiscere/fōtum/æt. His feet contextually refers to the fisherman. Familiar finite indicatives do not make either subordinate construction taught.
Supply mid mildheortnesse as manner and the prefixed verb ūpāhōf. Hē is the fisherman; hine is Apollonius.

support_groups.local_meaning: And led him with him to his house.
support_groups.scope_note: Supply mid him accompaniment and tō his hūse destination. Hine is Apollonius; him and his contextually refer to the fisherman. Hūs is not in the active prior lexicon and must be supplied.

support_groups.local_meaning: And set before him the provisions that he had to offer him.
support_groups.scope_note: Supply ēstas, lęgde, dative him beforan, object-relative ðe, and the available-to-offer habban construction. Tō bēodanne morphology is new Unit6, offer sense prior, but the object/recipient availability frame remains supplied. The second him is Apollonius, not a reflexive recipient.

support_groups.local_meaning: He still wanted, according to his ability, to show him greater kindness.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Adjectivally used participles agree in gender, number and case, with the strong/weak choices already taught for adjectives. Present -ende follows the grēne-type strong declension; it is not a masculine agent noun in -end.

Cook61: present participles in the predicate as nominative/accusative are generally uninflected. Cook62: predicate past participles are generally indeclinable or take strong masculine endings. Cook179 allows uninflected predicate participles. Thus neuterplural dēor bunden is acceptable; dēor bundene is also licensed in verbal passive usage. Do not judge them by an obligatory attributive neuter-u rule.

Heavy-stem disyllabic participles can lose the unstressed vowel before vowel-initial inflections: bundenes→bundnes, bundenum→bundnum; hīeredes→hīerdes, hīeredum→hīerdum, hīerede→hīerde. Full vowels are often restored in West Saxon. Keep the full stem before -ne/-re/-ra; doubled n in bundenne is ordinary. Short-root fręmed/nęred and lufod retain their vowel in the selected model. Rare -u cells above are transparently paradigm-derived.

Weak participles are lexical principal parts, not a universal past-minus-e shortcut: hīerde→hīered, fręmede→fręmed, lufode→lufod, sealde→seald, worhte→worht, sętte→sętt, sęnde→sęnd, lǣdde→lǣd. Before inflection, syncope can bring a dental into contact with a voiceless stem and cause -t-, as Fulk113 scierped→scierpte. These audit examples do not newly assign unlisted verbs.

A past participle of an intransitive verb need not be passive. Source wæs geworden is a become/come-to-pass resultative closure, not a transitive passive. Auxiliary tense does not force one Modern English tense/aspect translation.

Form direct yes/no and interrogative questions, govern interrogative case by its function, distinguish hū and hwȳ, and apply common clause-order tendencies without dummy do or a rigid universal formula.
Use invariant ðe, inflected demonstrative relatives and demonstrative plus ðe; distinguish antecedent case from internal relative case and preserve personal-antecedent verb agreement.

Use complete ætēowian present/preterite indicative and subjunctive, complete scīnan subjunctives, both geblētsian commands, productive count plural līf and the bounded cognate-accusative, fill and control constructions.

recognition_outcomes: Recognize documented hwām and distinct instrumental reference forms while lexical hwȳ why remains separately productive; general instrumental syntax is not assigned.

bounded_scope: Course Units1–7 are the sole prior-teaching authority.

Direct questions and ordinary subject/object/dative relatives are productive. Main-clause and relative-clause cases are independently governed in the assigned model. Case attraction is a limited recognition note; embedded interrogatives and extended content-clause syntax remain later work.
Hwā/hwæt has singular common-personal and neuter columns only. The nominal instrumental reference forms do not establish general instrumental syntax; lexical hwȳ why is separately bounded.
Full hwilc, hwæðer and hūlic morphology supports ordinary direct interrogative uses; hwæðer is practised attributively with a supplied two-person context, without a new partitive construction.
Existing se/ðes morphology, eall and ǣlc, and ōðer second retain their actual prior milestones. New relative and other/another senses require explicit teaching.
New sum, ǣnig, gehwilc and swilc uses are ordinary attributive certain/some, any, each and such; ilca is weak only and self has complete strong/weak morphology with bounded emphasis/reflexive use.

Cook§89 indefinite ān a/certain, negative/either families, indeclinable anything/nothing families, -hwega formations and broad free-choice/partitive patterns are explicitly deferred to Unit15. Prior cardinal ān does not teach its indefinite sense.
Līf plural morphology is promoted for individual lives and the explicitly taught libban cognate-accusative frame. Gefyllan fill is distinct from finish/accomplish; prior supplied history is retained.

Ætēowian has complete assigned indicative and subjunctive systems; scīnan has complete new subjunctives; geblētsian has both new commands. Familiar verb headwords do not supply missing moods or commands.
The exact Cook hint gesęte remains supplied with a bounded placement-in-location explanation. No independent prefixed gesettan system is assigned.
The habban...on...gewealde control frame is taught separately from spatial on and under. Geweald singular is prior; its plural remains recognition-only.

All72 exact merchant words, four complete turns and15 original notes are retained. The12 local helps support source-only maritime vocabulary, content clause, useful-datives, correlator, collective hit and accompanying participle; those supplied dependencies are never tested for unaided recall.

The62word new dialogue and16 examples are declared new teaching material. Their public text has independent source and grammar checks; all answer models and ordered output tokens stay in the clearly named author-only file.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Hwā/hwæt has singular morphology only. The masculine/feminine series is shared: hwā, hwæs, hwǣm, hwone; neuter hwæt, hwæs, hwǣm, hwæt. Do not invent plural or separate feminine forms. Cook also prints hwām for the dative; it is a valid recognized alternative to selected hwǣm.
audited_inflection_rules.scope: Eight productive NGDA cells. Distinct hwȳ/hwon instrumentals remain reference; lexical hwȳ why is separately productive.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Use the full strong NGDA endings with each listed lexical stem: masculine singular zero/-es/-um/-ne; neuter zero/-es/-um/zero; feminine selected zero or -u/-re/-re/-e; masculine plural -e/-ra/-um/-e; neuter selected zero or -u/-ra/-um/zero or -u; feminine plural -a/-ra/-um/-a. Feminine plural -e is a valid broader strong-adjective alternative, already established in the course; the selected matrices consistently use -a. Gender/number/case still agree with the modified noun or referent.
audited_inflection_rules.scope: Complete24 logical cells per selected strong model; distinct masculine/neuter singular instrumental -e is reference, not general instrumental production.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Selected feminine nominative singular and neuter nominative/accusative plural are sumu, but hwilc, hūlic, gehwilc, swilc and self. The selected ǣnig model retains -u as ǣnigu; the analogical zero-ending ǣnig is a recognized alternative. These listed outcomes govern production; a learner must not infer the entire disyllabic pattern from modern-looking spelling or from one familiar adjective.
audited_inflection_rules.scope: Short sum has -u; heavy/selected zero-ending models and the explicit ǣnig alternative remain distinct. Cook and Wright state variation and analogy, so no universal spelling-only rule is asserted.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Hwæðer selects hwæðr- before the ordinary vowel endings: hwæðres, hwæðrum, hwæðre, hwæðra. Retain e before consonantal endings: hwæðerne, hwæðerre, hwæðerra. Attested hwæðeres and simplified feminine hwæðere are valid variants; they do not replace the selected matrix.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Ilca is weak only. Its stem ilc- takes masculine nominative singular -a; feminine/neuter nominative singular and neuter accusative singular -e; other singular NGDA cells -an; plural nominative/accusative -an, genitive -ra, dative -um. Apply the same endings to self- for the weak self model; retain the separate strong self matrix.
audited_inflection_rules.scope: Two complete24-cell weak systems. Weak-only ilca must not acquire an invented strong ilc paradigm. Weak instrumental is syncretic with dative and gains no general syntax here.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: Ðe is invariant. The inflected relative se/sēo/ðæt reuses every prior NGDA form, alone or followed by ðe. In the selected ordinary construction, its case follows its internal role while gender/number track the antecedent; the antecedent's external case can differ. In a possessive relative, genitive marks possession within the relative clause (English whose/of whom/of which); its gender and number still refer back to the antecedent, not to the possessed noun. This uses the already productive demonstrative genitives and does not promote earlier first/second-person personal genitives or general instrumentals. Case attraction is an attested recognition exception, not assigned production.
audited_inflection_rules.scope: Ordinary subject, possessive, direct-object and governed/recipient functions; relative verb person/number follows the antecedent where relevant. ðe+personal pronoun is a bounded recognition strategy.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: The recognition ge-compound uses the interrogative-type singular pattern: gehwā/gehwæt, gehwæs, gehwǣm, gehwone/gehwæt. No plural is invented.
audited_inflection_rules.scope: Eight NGDA recognition cells; ordinary/partitive/distributive independent production remains Unit15. Other indefinite families have explicit dispositions.

audited_inflection_rules.rule: WeakII ætēowian keeps the lexical ætēow- stem. Present indicative ætēowie, ætēowast, ætēowað, plural ætēowiað; preterite ætēowode, ætēowodest, ætēowode, plural ætēowodon. Present subjunctive singular ætēowie/plural ætēowien; preterite singular ætēowode/plural ætēowoden. Every plural/subject-person cell is explicitly recorded. original_notes.text: Lat. mercator. Other Old English terms for merchant are cīepa and cīepmann. From a collateral form of the latter, cēapmann, without umlaut, is derived Mod. Eng. chapman. How is chap- related to cheap? See the New English Dictionary (New Eng. Dict.) under these words.
Lat. utilis. Cf. the Mod. Eng. noun behoof.

Carlyle (Sartor Resartus, Bk. 3, Chap. 7) has the following: “König (King), anciently Könning, means Ken-ning (Cunning), or which is the same thing, Can-ning. Ever must the Sovereign of Mankind be fitly entitled King.” On the other hand Gummere (Germanic Origins, p. 270): “At the head of the family we found, of course, the father; and at the head of the state we naturally look for the king. The word ‘king’ means the child or son of the tribe, its representative or even creation; man of race, man of rank. Gradually the king ceases to be regarded as a creation of his race; his ancestry is pushed back to the gods, and his right is quite above all sanctions of popular choice or approval.” Which of these views is confirmed by etymology?
Lat. periculo. Mod. Eng. form of pliht?
Lat. vix vivus evadens. Note the love for alliteration, even in the Latin.

local_support.explanation: mangere, masculine, merchant; the nominative form is used in addressing him.

local_support.source_phrase: ðæt behēfe ic eom; And hū?
local_support.explanation: I say that I am useful. This ðæt introduces a content clause; it is not the neuter demonstrative or a relative. behēfe means useful and takes the dative people to whom the merchant is useful. The next question And hū? abbreviates And how [are you useful]?; its omitted predicate is recovered from this answer. That exact ellipsis is supplied here, without teaching unrestricted question ellipsis.

local_support.source_phrase: ge cyninge and ealdormannum, and weligum, and eallum folce
local_support.explanation: ge ... and coordinates the recipients: both to the king and to nobles, and to wealthy people, and to all the people. cyninge is dative singular; ealdormannum and weligum are dative plural; folce is dative singular. weligum is an adjective used substantivally.

local_support.source_phrase: āstīge mīn scip mid hlæstum mīnum
local_support.explanation: I board my ship with my cargo. āstīge is first singular present; scip is accusative, the thing boarded. mid governs dative hlæstum mīnum here. hlæst is neuter and is plural in this cargo expression.
I row over sea regions / across stretches of sea. rōwe is first singular present; sǣlice dǣlas is accusative masculine plural after spatial ofer.

local_support.source_phrase: cīepe mīn ðing, and bycge ðing dēorwierðu
local_support.explanation: I sell my goods and buy valuable things. cīepe and bycge are first singular presents. Both ðing phrases are accusative plural; mīn and dēorwierðu agree with neuter plural ðing.

local_support.source_phrase: ðā on ðissum lande ne bēoð ācęnnede
local_support.explanation: which are not produced in this land. The target relative ðā is nominative neuter plural, the subject inside its clause; its antecedent ðing is accusative in the main clause. lande is dative singular, neuter land. ācęnnede is a plural predicate past participle, are produced; its exact form is supplied, without assigning the whole verb or a general participial declension.

I bring it/the goods here to you. tōgelǣde is first singular present. ēow is dative plural recipient. hit is the actual neuter singular object used collectively for the merchandise; translate its reference, not as a new unrelated object. hider expresses movement hither.

at great risk across the sea. mid has a supplied circumstance use here and governs dative masculine singular miclum plihte. In ofer sǣ, sǣ has the same singular form in the accusative and dative. Across the sea motivates an accusative extent interpretation in this context, but the written form does not prove that case. No unique accusative answer is required from this surface alone; the task concerns the meaning across the sea.
sometimes I suffer shipwreck. hwīlum is a frequency adverb; forlidennesse is accusative feminine singular, the object of first singular present ðolie.
with the loss of all my things. lyre is dative masculine singular after mid; ealra ðinga mīnra is a genitive plural dependent of loss.

barely escaping alive. unēaðe means with difficulty/barely; cwic is nominative masculine singular referring to the merchant; ætberstende is a nominative singular present participle expressing his accompanying circumstance. The construction and exact forms are supplied.
